George "Red" Sylvester Callender (Patricia Willard) --
(August 13, 1981):

....[FIRST MINUTE NOT AUDIBLE]... For some reason, my mother went to Boston to work, I think, during that time, for a private family or something. And my father was a steward on a ship at that time. And they met. And so, I was conceived in Boston, but afterwards they married, of course -- they had to be very up to par. Anyway, my mother went to Virginia and I had me, and two months later they took me back to Boston, and after that back to Virginia. I remember staying in Virginia until I was about 3, and then we moved to Atlantic City. My memory is excellent...

Yes, we went to Atlantic City, and when I was 5, I went into the First Grade -- skipped the kindergarten. So I was always the youngest one. Even in later years, when I started playing in bands, I was the youngest one. But now that's changed completely! [LAUGHS]
To go back to the beginning: Is the birth-date that is in all these reference books the correct one?
March 6, 1918. [IN Unfinished Dream: The Musical World of Red Callender, HE CITES MARCH 6, 1916]
I want to confirm that one. And it was Richmond, Virginia.
Callender (#1) - 2

Richmond, Virginia. Yes, that's where I was born. Not actually in Richmond; Richmond is a city. But my folks had a farm outside of Richmond, and actually it was called Haynesville, Post Office. I remember that. There was a screen through the back, which is not important to this, but anyhow I can remember it. I used to go back there and fish with my grandfather, who would take a bent pin and put a worm on it, and go back in the stream and fish -- he'd catch catfish. I remember being a little guy, I got stuck in a thing...those things that come out of the catfish...
I never caught a catfish... Yes, I think I did, come to think of it.
Well, if you've seen a catfish, then you know those...
Yes.

They look like whiskers. But anyhow, I got stuck with one, and I've been pretty shy ever since. So years later, when I took my family fishing, I used to put gloves on. They'd laugh at me. I'd put rubber gloves on. So finally I got so I could touch a worm again. Which has nothing to do with music, but all that happened.
Well, no, this is your life, and your life in music -- it's all of your life that you want to talk
Callender (#1) - 3
about. About your mother and your father, can we have their names on their tape?

My mother's maiden name was Hattie Lee Spense, and my father's name was George Lawrence Callender. So although my name is George Sylvester Callender... I'm a junior, but I guess that wouldn't be approved on me because my middle name is different than my father's. But anyhow, they used to call me George Junior Callender. And I can remember when I first went to school and my father took me, and said, "George Callender, Junior," and I said, "no, my name is George Junior Callender." I finally figured it out that my name was George Callender, Junior, with Sylvester in the middle.
When you mentioned the Sylvester in the beginning, that was from the Bajan?

Yes, the Sylvester part is the Bajan, or Barbados. That's a popular name in Barbados. And incidentally, we were in Barbados a few years ago. It's a small island, 21 miles long and 14 miles wide at the largest part. And in the phone book, Callender could compare to Smith here; it's mostly Callenders in Barbados.
Oh, that's interesting.
Yes. And we have an historian, as a matter of fact, a family historian. On Labor Day the Callender
Callender (#1) - 4

clan meets in Lunenberg(?), Massachusetts. My first cousin on my father's side has this family meeting every year, and Callenders from all over the country and Barbados get together. I haven't been yet, because I've been a little too busy on Labor Days to go. But there's another meeting this year.

And what I had started to say is that our family traces back to 1700, when five brothers, for whatever reason, had to leave Scotland, and they settled in the Caribbean, and married Indian women, African women and mulatto women and all sorts of women. I guess that's why you'd call me a real mongrel. Here I am, whatever color I am, I have freckles...
And red hair.
...and red hair. And it all dates back to some Callender in Scotland.
How fascinating.
You didn't know that, did you.
I didn't know that. No, I didn't know. I didn't know that Callender was a Bajan name. I didn't know about all the Callenders in Barbados.
Yeah. The difference in the Callenders would be in the spelling. Now, all of the Scotch descendants spelled the name Callender, the Irish descendants are Callendair. So that's why my name gets
Callender (#1) - 5

screwed up so much in the spelling. I can write my name on something and give it somebody with the "e" real big on the end, and it will come back "Callendar." So I used to get real teed-off about it, but I guess I'm getting used to it now. So long as they call me, I don't care how they spell it.
And sometimes they don't get both "L's" in it, too.
Frequently!
I've seen it spelled like the calendar.
Yeah, they hear Callender, and they immediately think of a date "Calendar," and it's not like that at all.
How do you spell Bajan?
Bajan. They say Bajin and it's spelled Bajan. That's a West Indian accent.
How do you spell Haynesville?
Haynesville. That's just a Post Office Box, and my grandfather's farm was just a few miles from there.
What was your grandfather's name?
My grandfather's name was Edmond Spense, and my grandmother's name was... I'll have to come back to that. She died a long time ago. [AMANDA TOLLS SPENSE]
That was your maternal grandparents.
Callender (#1) - 6
My maternal grandparents.
And your paternal grandparents?
My paternal grandparents... I never saw my grandfather, although I know all about him now. His name was Benjamin. And my paternal grandmother's name was Adelaide.
Did they live in the Islands?
Yes, they never left the Islands. There's many branches of the family. I have a... Later I'll show you. I have a... What do you call it? You can lay it out on the floor and you can see all of the...
Genealogy?

Genealogy, yeah; the family tree. My daughters, Sharon and Sylvia, and my wife, Mary Lou, and I, went down there five years ago. It didn't matter it me, but they were interested, so they went to the Hall of Records and found my father's birth certificate, where he was baptized and the whole bit. So it gives one a sense of family pride.
Right.
Anyhow, we knew where we came from, which is pretty wild. This happened before Roots, too.
You went to school, then in...
Callender (#1) - 7

I went to school in Atlantic City. The New Jersey Avenue School first, then Indiana Avenue School, and later Pennsylvania Avenue School. And a funny thing: At that time, the schools were integrated -- when I was a kid. And a bunch of Negro doctors got together and decided they wanted their own schools, which in retrospect was very silly. You know, really. But they got their wish, and so they made their own segregation.
Oh.
You didn't know that either.
I didn't know that either.
Well, most people don't know that, but that happened in Atlantic City in the early Twenties.
Was there music in your home?

My mother used to fool with the guitar, and my uncle played Blues on the guitar and sing the Blues. But my earliest recollection of hearing sound was an old Victrola or gramophone, whichever it was called, and this particular piece sticks in my mind. They had a lot of Bert Williams records and Paul Whiteman records. And I remember one thing that caught me was a violin solo, (?) Meditation, I think by Massenet. I guess I must have been no more than three years old when this captured me, and I used to sit and listen to this all day.
Callender (#1) - 8

So in later years in Atlantic City when I was going to school, I remember one day standing outside of a tavern and hearing "Black and Tan Fantasy" (I didn't know who it was at the time, but naturally later I found it was Duke Ellington) and the "East Toodle-Oo," and I think that's what really turned me on to be a musician.

So Bordentown School up in Bordentown, New Jersey, which was about 19 miles from Trenton, had a band that used to travel all over the state, they came to our school, and after hearing this band I just had to go. Fortunately, my parents were able to send me to this school. And that was my beginning as a musician. My teacher there was Alexander Valentine, who had been to Europe with Jim Europe. Everybody remembers Jim Europe.
Right.

Well, he had been the trombone player in the Jim Europe band, and he and W.C. Handy had been great friends. And I remember when I got out of high school and got my little piece of paper, I thought... You know, I had studied composition and arranging and copying music; I thought I could get a job as a copyist. So he gave me a note to meet Mr. Handy; I think he was at 1619 Broadway in New York. So I go to Mr. Handy's office, and I hand him my little piece of paper, and he studied me a long time and
Callender (#1) - 9

said, "You know, son, this office is just a front; I just come here to get away from home. I've been making my living off 'St. Louis Blues' for the past forty years." So I never did get a job as a copyist, which was probably fortunate, because I continued studying.

Charlie Shavers and Dizzy Gillespie both went to this school. Dizzy was a bad boy; Dizzy got kicked out of school. He hasn't changed a bit either. Dizzy was always dizzy, you know, kind of a devil, always doing nutty things. But anyhow...
How old were you when you started going to this school?
I was 12 years old when I went to this school?
And how old were you when you heard "Black and Tan Fantasy"?

Oh, I was about 10 years old. In fact, I pushed my age up. I wasn't quite 12 when I went to school. That was the minimum. You had to be 12. So I pushed my age up. I lied about it, said that I was a little older. So I got in school. I was always rather tall for my age, although I was very skinny at the time.
But I fell in love with the brass instruments. First I tried the trumpet, the trombone, and then the tuba. I just
Callender (#1) - 10

had to hear that sound. So down the road in a place called White Hill, one of the guys in school whose name was Dwight Boone, had an old bass fiddle, so he brought this bass fiddle to school. That was my introduction to the bass fiddle, which was very close to the tuba -- just a matter of months apart. So I always say I started both at the same time, although the tuba actually came first.
And you were how old when you started with the tuba?
I was 12 years old.
Oh, immediately on going to that school you started with the tuba.

Immediately I started with the tuba. And, well, the alto horn; I played an alto horn, too. But the tuba was my love. I used to lay under our old Majestic radio and listen to Duke Ellington and Paul Whiteman (they used to broadcast every night, you know), and all I could hear was the tuba and the bass. At that time, Duke had a tuba, too. I imagine you have some of those old records.
Yes.

Yeah, so... I don't know whether it was Wellman Braud or not. The first time I actually saw the band, Wellman Braud was playing bass, and I used to sit in front of the band in awe, digging these guys. Years later,
Callender (#1) - 11
when Blanton... Blanton and I became friends. I'm jumping ahead now many years.
That's all right.

Blanton and I became friends. As a matter of fact, when Blanton got sick... Well, we were good friends. I was with him the day before he died. Lee Young and I and Billy Strayhorn; you know, we used to hang out together. At that time, I was working with Lee in Lester's band... I'm jumping around, but that's the way it comes.
That's okay.
I was working with Lee in Lester Young's band at the Capri...
This is Billy Berg's club, right?

Billy Berg's Capri. And Elmer Fain said, 'Hey, do you want to go with Duke?' And I said, 'Wow, that's wonderful, but I really would rather stay here and learn more about music.' Because I knew if I went with Duke, I'd never get to play my tuba and I'd never get to write. And I was writing for Lee and Lester's band, and I also wrote for a lot of bands... I used to write for shows around town.
But before that, let me to 19...
Go ahead, jump around.
Callender (#1) - 12

Okay, I have to. Because before that.. When I mentioned Elmer Fain it makes me think of my first encounter with Louis Armstrong, which was on the 13th of November, 1937. I guess I was still a teenager. Anyhow, Pops Foster got sick, and I guess I was new in town then... Anyhow, Elmer Fain said, "Hey, kid, I got a job for you." I said, "What?" He said, "Louis Armstrong needs a bass player." So they were playing at the Vogue Ballroom on 9th and Grand in Los Angeles. You may remember that, too. But anyhow, they were playing, and I went with the band making $85 a week. This was the day after I had bought one of the same basses I have now. Luis Russell was the bandleader, and in the band was Paul Barbarin, Red Allen, Charlie Holmes, and Luis Russell playing piano -- and naturally Pops. I think Pops was 36 or 37 at the time. I was there when he married Lucille, too.
Oh.
You didn't know that?
No, there's a lot I don't know!
Anyhow, that was one of the thrills of my life. We had the white (?) uniforms and making $85 a week; I'd never heard of that kind of money!
Oh, that was good. Awfully good.
Callender (#1) - 13

Oh, that was great. Well, I think I stayed there a month or six weeks, then Pops Foster came back, and I resumed my... I can call it a "career" now, although at the time I was just having fun. I was determined to be a good musician.

Around that same time, Cab Calloway's band was out here, and Al Morgan went with the... Al Morgan had quit Cab's band. And I remember being hired for a gig out in Gardenia, at a place called Gloria Nightclub. C.C. Caldwell had the band. And I was hired for this gig, so I go out to the gig, and I get to the door, and I hear a bass in there tuning up. I wonder what's happening. So I go to the door with my little bass, and Al Morgan is on the stand, and they say to me, "Sorry, kid, we got Al Morgan."
Oh.
Well, you know, those kinds of things hurt, but it didn't hurt so much that it didn't give me more determination than ever to show them. And years later, I did show them.
What happened?
Well, I managed to become a fairly decent bass player and tuba player, and work in the studios..
Oh, yeah. I thought maybe you meant some specific incident with them.
Callender (#1) - 14

No, not with them. But those things hurt, and at the time they happen you say, 'I'll show them.' So I did. But it didn't feel so good when I showed them, you know I just went on to be a better musician than I'd probably have been if they had hired me. Because those guys believed in staying on the job year-in and year-out, and I knew you couldn't learn anything like that. So consequently, I can't ever consider myself as having had a steady job. I figured the more I know about music, the more I'll be able to work. So having a steady job has never worried me. I've always been able to work.
At that very young age, was that brief time with Louis Armstrong a learning experience for you?
Oh yes, indeed.
In what way?

Well, you see, at that time people were surprised when bass players or drummers could read music. But I had learned to read before I ever could play an instrument, so that was one advantage. Well, yeah, that gave me...
You were mentioning Elmer Fain. What was his function at that time? Now he's a business agent of the...
He was a business agent at that point.
Callender (#1) - 15
Oh, he was then, too.

At that time there were two locals, a Black local and a White local. 767 was the Black local and 747 was the White local. The White local was located on Georgia Street in downtown Los Angeles, and the Black local was on Central Avenue and 18th Street. It's easy to remember, because Lester Young's family lived right next door to the Local. As a matter of fact, from the upstairs you could get out of the window...and I've done it, to hop across to the roof of where Lester lived. He and I were good friends, too. This was after he'd gotten out of the Army, and I guess he never did get over the depression that that Army scene caused him.
Did he ever talk about it to you?

Yeah. He would tell me some of the things... At that time, I guess he'd... Well, anybody who smoked pot was considered a dope fiend. So he was considered a dope fiend! And naturally he resented that, because he wasn't! He was an ordinary person like the rest of us. I mean, who didn't smoke pot? I certainly did. Although at this point, I smoke very little of anything -- and drink very little of anything. Because I have seen so many guys, like... Well, I saw what happened to Lester, his frustrations and feeling bruised... And I guess it's true.
Callender (#1) - 16

He was, you know, such a great talent who wasn't really recognized or rewarded for what he could really do. But he used to get a big punch-bowl and take a bottle of sauterne wine and a quart of gin, and put it in there, and that's how he'd start his day off.
From the time he came out of the Army?

Mmmm-hmmm, yeah. And he would eat very little. Although he was playing beautifully, and still played beautifully at that time. But I guess he... I don't know whether he had a death wish or what it was, but frustration, I suppose, had a lot to do with it.
But he was like a different person after he came out...
Oh, man.
That's what I've heard people say.

Well, he was always... I loved him. He was a beautiful soft-spoken person who never seemed to get angry at anybody. All he wanted to do was to play his horn, which he did so beautifully. But we were working at the Capri at this time, and the union wouldn't let him... He had to wait a six-month period. So the band would play, and then he would come up and do a specialty. They called it a specialty, because he wasn't allowed to be on the bandstand
Callender (#1) - 17
during the whole set -- which was some silly rule, but nonetheless it applied.

So I guess it was through him that Barney Josephson and Cafe Society heard about us, and hired us to come to New York. This is funny. Out here... This was during the War. Was it? Yeah, during the War. Out here we worked from 10 to 2, four hours a night, which was nice. So we found out we were getting forty or fifty dollars a week more to go to the Cafe Society in New York. But we didn't know that in New York you worked from 8 to 4.
Gee!

Eight hours! But that was fun. And anyhow, at the Cafe Society Downtown at this time there was a group called the Reviewers. Judy Holiday was a member of the group, who later became a big star. Pete Johnson and Albert Ammons were the two boogie-woogie pianists, and the show also had a Classical pianist, Sam Reichman Lewis he was called. This was, you know, a lot of fun, although the hours were really ridiculous. Because when you'd get off at 4 o'clock in the morning in New York, you know, you'd go out and eat, and it would always be daylight when I'd get home, and consequently it was just one... You know, you'd get enough sleep to come back to work and the same routine. So
Callender (#1) - 18
from that standpoint, I never did dig working in New York, because the hours are too long.
Well, did your group alternate with these others...
Yes.
You didn't have to be the rhythm section for everybody.

Oh, no, we alternated with everybody. But the hours... We played three or four sets a night. But just standing around in between was, you know, pretty terrible. And I found out later that Leonard Feather lived upstairs over it at Number 2 Sheridan Square; he lived right over the place. That's I guess when he had... He was relatively new here then, too.

So we worked out the contract, and rather than come back to Los Angeles I formed a trio with Sir Charles Thompson on piano and Louis Gonsales. I hadn't mentioned him, but he was a guitarist in Lee and Lester's band. I hadn't mentioned who was in the band either. It was Paul Campbell, trumpet; Bumps Myers, Hubert Myers, tenor and Lester, tenor; and Jimmy Rowles was playing piano. But Benny Goodman stole Jimmy Rowles from us, so when we went in to New York, Clyde Hart came into the band and did the whole engagement until just when we were almost ready to leave,
Callender (#1) - 19
and then Sir Charles came in. I guess Lee and Lester both went back to California, and I decided I was going to strike out on my own. So I formed the trio, and...
What year was that?

That was '44 or '45, somewhere in there. I signed up with the William Morris Agency, and they booked my little trio. We worked upstate New York through Ohio, and all kind of crazy little gigs. We'd play our little music and sing songs, you know. I guess everybody tried to emulate King Cole at the time, and we were no exception.
You were singing?
Oh, yeah.
I didn't know you sang.
Well, I don't consider myself a singer, but I can carry a tune. [LAUGHS]
I would guess that you probably could.

So all during this period I wasn't playing my tuba at all, because, you know, it was enough hassle carrying the bass around. I don't think I picked the tuba up again until some years later. Matter of fact, yeah, I picked the tuba up after I had gone to... I'm jumping around again.
That's okay.
Callender (#1) - 20
[END OF TAPE 1, SIDE A]

So the trio went on for a while. Then I came back to Los Angeles and I really got deeply into the recording scene, and that's how I guess I managed to record with so many people -- Wardell Gray, Dexter Gordon, Charlie Parker, Erroll Garner and Bumps Myers.

And then I was working for... I was an A&R man for a record company...I can't think of the company...but Jack Lauderdale was the President of the company, and he hired me as an A&R man. So Clark Terry, who was a friend, said, "Hey, I got a guy I want you to hear." So Lauderdale and I get into his Cadillac, and drive back to St. Louis to listen to Jimmy Forrest. So Jimmy Forrest played... I said, "Hey, let's record this guy." (I'll get to the rest in a second.) I said, "Hey, let's record it. This is wonderful." So Lauderdale had some ladies he wanted to see in Chicago, so he said, "No, we can pick up something in Chicago." So we go to Chicago, and two months later, "Night Train" comes out. This was what Lauderdale had passed up. I wanted to do it, and he was too busy to get to see some ladies, and he let that one get by. And I never let him forget it.
Didn't "Night Train" happen after Jimmy Forrest had already worked in Duke's band?
Callender (#1) - 21
Yes.
Is that where Clark knew him from, in Duke's band?
Oh, no. Clark knew him before that. You see, Clark is originally from St. Louis...
Because you know, there is a difference of opinion between "Night Train" and "Happy Go Lucky Local."
Well, it's the same thing!
Sure it is. But I mean, there's a difference of opinion about who wrote what.
Oh, well, Duke wrote "Happy Go Lucky Local", and Jimmy Forrest just...
Left with it. Or something.
...just lifted it. Duke didn't seem to care.
Well, Duke cared.
Oh, did he?
But Duke wasn't into suing people. He never sued anybody.
So he just let it go.
Yeah. He would, you know, make remarks about it, but...
But he never did a thing about it.
Callender (#1) - 22

No. He would just say, "This is a number we wrote," and then he would give the date, and he would sometimes say how many years before "Night Train" it was that we wrote and recorded this, and then he would play "Happy Go Lucky Local." But that's as far as he would...

Oh, it was probably ten or twelve years before "Night Train." Oh, it was an open secret. Everybody knew Duke wrote it. But Jimmy Forrest recorded it and put his name on it, and... Well, he got the credit for "Night Train." But everybody knows that it was "Happy Go Lucky Local" that knew anything about Duke Ellington.

How come when Basie played it, when Jimmy Forrest was in Basie's band, at the end of Jimmy Forrest's solo Basie would always say, "And the composer of 'Night Train,'" and Jimmy Forrest would take ten bows.
Well, everybody knew it. I guess it got to be a joke actually. Because Jimmy Forrest got away with it.
Yes, he did.
Well, I guess Duke was a bigger man than a lot of people realize, in a lot of ways. Because he didn't have to let it go. He just said, "What the hell. It can't hurt me that much."
Whereas on the other hand, I think, Juan Tizol sued Perez Prado, when Perez Prado got a hit with
Callender (#1) - 23
"Patricia", which Juan said was his "Perdido" at a different tempo.
That's true. It was.
But Duke wouldn't sue.
No. And I understand now that Barney Bigard is reaping the rewards of "Mood Indigo."
Finally. Well, Barney got a little bit of it.
A little bit.
But it was twenty years before Barney got his name on..
Yeah. Irving Mills' name was on it and everybody except Barney, who actually wrote it.
Right. And it was the twenty years when it was the biggest hit that Barney didn't get any royalties.
But now it's a hit again, and Dottie is doing beautifully.
I'm so glad.
Yeah, me too. She deserves.
Absolutely. But at least Barney had the satisfaction of...
Of knowing.
...of getting his name there and knowing that he finally got the credit he was supposed to have.
Callender (#1) - 24
yes. So there is justice.
Not always on time, but yes.
No, not always on time. But you see, a lot of those things... Should we...
It's all right.

Well, a lot of things in the band came out of riffs, and the guys would set a riff and Duke would just write them down! Then the guys later got bitter because they didn't have brains enough to write them down.

Yeah, I'm sure that's where a lot of it came from. And sometimes Duke would put their names on it and sometimes Duke wouldn't put their names on it. That was sort of the way the band worked. And he took from those around him, and then those around him sometimes from him -- and that's the way it went.

Well, he was I guess the loosest bandleader there ever was. He didn't care... That's what I saw. If he had a bass player and a drummer, he'd start anyway. And I know a lot of the wild sounds came about that way. Like, maybe the third alto player or Johnny wouldn't be there, so the trombone, being in the register, although...you just change the clef sign, and it's the same thing. Somebody would take an alto saxophone part, and it would sound... You know, wild sounds! I know how they happened. A lot of
Callender (#1) - 25
people figured it was on purpose, and sometimes it was just accidentally.
And he loved those accidents.
Yes!
Well, he explained it once by saying, "We are Primitive artists. We employ the materials at hand."

And he was so right. Oh! Well, he was my musical godfather. The last thing he said to me... I saw him at Disneyland, and the last words he said to me was, "Hey, when are you going on the road with me?" And that was the last time I saw him alive, too. Mary Lou and I were on a plane headed to New York, we were going on the first Jazz cruise, and the news flashed on the plane that Duke Ellington had just passed. So a couple of days later we... He was laying in state. I've forgotten the mortuary. But we went in the morning and sat there practically all day, and thousands of people just came by him. Because he was really musical royalty.
Well, the whole city of New York was in mourning. You might not have known it out here. Because I went, and...
Well, I was there and I saw it, yeah. It was...
Callender (#1) - 26
It was like a world leader had passed. Which, you know, he was!
He was a world leader.
But I think it was appropriate. The entire city reacted.
Yeah, the city was in mourning for a few days. And I was happy that I was able to have been in his presence.
He asked you more than one time to join the band, right?
Yeah.
How many times? Do you remember?

Oh, it was maybe two or three times, whenever he'd have a bass problem. But the fact that he thought enough of me to want me in his band really satisfied my ego, because he might have let me play the tuba and do the things I wanted to do, but I didn't think there was much of a chance for me to do much writing for Duke Ellington. So I stuck to my guns. I have no regrets. Just the fact that he wanted me was enough.
You sat in with the band a few times.
Yeah.
I remember, I think, at the Oasis you...
Callender (#1) - 27
At the Oasis, when Wendell Marshall... Yeah, I sat in with the band. And the funny thing about that band, there was no bass book, you know...
That was true of several chairs.
Yeah. [LAUGHS] I'd say, "Where's the music?" He'd say, "Oh, you'll hear it."
Even when Wendell was there, there was no bass book, right?

Well, a smattering of a book. But things like "Cottontail" and "Perdido" and "Caravan" and those kind of things, stuff where you think there would be a part, there was no part. So he'd start, and I'd just play what I heard.
Well, that's what he liked.
