Well, there you go. Do you want to leave Mingus now and go somewhere else?
Unless there's some particular recollection you have that might be of interest.
Well, there's many, many things. I had a band in San Francisco, and Mingus came to town so I hired him to play with my band. We had two basses. I might have mentioned that before.
I was going to ask you about that.

We played at a place called the Beige Room, on Powell, I think, in San Francisco. I loved it, but naturally they didn't understand what we were trying to do, whoever heard the two basses in the band. But since then Duke's had two basses in his band, and Charlie Barnet had two basses in his band... Maybe Duke had two before this, because this was in 1948 I'm talking about.
Duke had two basses right before Blanton came in, didn't he?
Right. Well, this was one of the times I had come back from Honolulu. I thought I'd come back and
live in the States again. So I stayed a few months. That's when I had the band in San Francisco.
Who else was in that band?

Teddy Edwards, Warren Bracken on piano, Bill Douglas I think was on drums in that band, and I had a trumpet player, Eddie...I can't think of his name at the moment either... Anyhow, I think there was about a six-piece band with two basses, which may have been ridiculous, but I liked it.
I wish I could have heard it.
Well, I say, some of the most interesting things have never been recorded, and that was one of those times.
And that was '48.
1948. I was living in Honolulu, but I came back for some reason.
Well, you came down to L.A. at some point around that time.
Yes.
The first time I heard you was... I was going to Los Angeles City College, and you did a concert there with Bob Fox, and it was around '49.
You were still a kid, yeah.
Yeah, I was still a kid.

Then I went back to Honolulu, and stayed until 1950. I mentioned that I played in a symphony, and I had my own band. Then I came back for something or other, because I had a family to take care of. I had one daughter, and I was responsible, so I had to come back and check things out every now and then.
Good.
Yeah. So I have no regrets about anything in that line. I took care of my obligations, and I'm very glad I did. It's made me able to look in the mirror and say, 'Hey, you did the best you could.'
Your son is how old now?
He's 26 the third of this month. Was it 25 or 26?
What year was he born?
How long has he been playing bass?

Well, he's been interested in music he was 7. I started him out with Bill Douglas. He wanted to play drums, so naturally he had all the best drum-sets, and he got to meet Buddy Rich and Louis Bellson and all those kind of people. But now he's playing the Fender bass, and he's built a recording studio in the garage, and he's playing a little piano. I still want him to go to school. He's doing

all this... He knows a little, but not nearly enough to be a complete musician. He just has a natural talent, and... I don't know whether being a Taurus or not has anything to do with it, but he's always a little guy that wanted to do it his way. He'd say when he was little, "I want to do it myself." Anyhow, he's written a few tunes, and some of it's beginning to sound pretty good.
Great. Does he still play drums?

Oh, yeah. He just bought a set from Earl Palmer. So now he's back playing the drums and doing his recording, you know, like Les Paul used to do... Les Paul used to do everything himself when he and Mary Ford used to do the multiple things. So now it's easy, you know. I think he's got about eight tracks to work with, so he puts down a line and overdubs it. Yeah, he's doing...
Earl Palmer has second-generation drums. Your son has Earl Palmer's drums, and I think Laura Bryant said her son was going to get a set of Earl Palmer's drums.
Well, we lived right around the corner from each other for a long time.
Yes, I remember. Not in Baldwin Hills...
In Baldwin Hills, yeah. Like, my last family is still there. Toni and April and Craig are still there. A funny thing, we were out in Thousand Oaks, we went

out there to have fun and play Sunday, and my oldest and my youngest daughter and their friend were staying with Toni in Baldwin Hills, so they all came out to function, and people were astounded that Mary Lou and Toni, you know, are friends.
I think that's wonderful!
Why not? And my teenage...my first wife... They're all friends. People can't understand this. To me it's great, you know?
Absolutely.

My daughter Sharon is the first one who got us all together. I call her Noel Coward, with the strange humor... She had a party, and Emma, my first wife, and Toni, my second wife, and my present wife, we were all at this party. Well, in the beginning I was a little uncomfortable, but I figured, 'What the hell?' I hadn't done bad by anybody. I left them all with nice houses.
Good for you.
Really!
I remember the lovely house you and Toni had in Baldwin Hills.
Yeah. So she's got nothing to beef about.
It's wonderful when people can all get along. Why not?
Why not?! You know, I've got no hate for anybody. We were all kids and we made a lot of mistakes. But that's history.
Right. Go ahead positively.
I say from this day forward. Yesterday I can't help.
[END OF CASSETTE #4, SIDE B]

You've brought this time the list of artists you have recorded and/or played with, which is, to say the least, extremely impressive. But besides that, what can you tell me about your musical experiences with... Shall we go down the list?
Well, let's see. I don't know how much tape you've got. I think you've got enough for this little story. This happened just the other night, and it has to do with Flip Wilson.
[PAUSE]

So we're all waiting in the cocktail lounge at United, and we're all sitting down having a cocktail, and Flip shows up with his recorder(?) or something like that on his back and his earphones. He says, "Hey, I'm glad to see you. I haven't seen you in a long time. You just look fine." So

we pass the usual B.S., he was looking good, too -- he'd picked up a few pounds. Anyway, he pulls me over to him and puts these things on my ears, like the Walkman, and he's got a whole raft of songs that he's written parodies to. For instance, he's done one to "Cry Me A River." His parody to that is "Fry Me A River."
Oh, Willie Bobo used to do that, I understand.

Oh, he did? Well, anyhow, he's got, you know, many of them, and he happens to be on his way to Chicago. So to cut the story short, my daughter is on standby, because she changed her reservation, and she's hoping she can get on this flight. So when 12:15 comes and he's getting ready to board, he says, "Well, aren't you going?" She said, "I'm on standby." He said, "no, you're not; you're with me." So he takes he on with him, and she called me to tell me that he took her on first-class with him, and told her things about how he relaxes to music, and how, you know, he replenishes his energies and all that, and when they get to Chicago he rents a limousine and takes her home in the limousine. Everything first-class.
That's beautiful.
Isn't that nice?
Yes, it certainly is. You worked the Flip Wilson Show...

I worked for four years with his show. And the reason that he wanted... Nobody had heard this before. Because when I worked with the show, Flip couldn't carry a tune in a basket. George Weill had to stand down in front and pull him in. You know, he'd point, "Come in now," and kind of guide him through these things. And we did, you know, stuff with Bing Crosby and Perry Como and all sorts of people. Flip was very insecure at the time with his singing, but he pulled it off because he's a hard worker. But now he's been really working. He's got an accompanist, and he's really got his act together. He can sing and keep tempo, and it's just wonderful. So he was telling, "Hey, he knows the difference." You know, he was pointing to me, telling everybody, "Yeah, he knows. He can tell. He knows the difference." And really, I have to say, discipline is what's done it. He's worked hard. Well, I already said the other part of this story. But this is how it all came about.
What years were those that you worked with Flip Wilson?
'71 up until '75.
Who else was in that band?

Oh, those who come to mind right off was Willie Green, Buddy Collette, Grover Mitchell, Conte Candoli, Buddy Childers, Irv Kotler playing drums, and... It was a big band. I can't think of all of them.
How big a band was it?

Oh, about a 15-16 piece band. You know, full reed section, full brass section, full rhythm section. Jimmy... God, I'm trying to think of the guitar player's name. A very shy guy. I can't think of the name now. I should have written these names down. I didn't know you were going to pop that on me.
Well, I didn't know we were going to be talking about Flip Wilson.
If we want to come back to it, I'll remember the names.

I just think it's interesting, and not many people away from the West Coast or the two Coasts realize how many really major Jazz musicians make their living, or used to when there were more bands on television, facelessly on the network television shows. There's only a couple that have bands any more, except for some of the specials. Right?
Well, the only big band is on the Johnny Carson Show. Merv Griffin has cut his band down to a small one.
Once in a while somebody will have a special with a big band.
Yeah. Well, when he goes to Vegas he hires a big band. But other than that, it's just a small group. Everybody is trying to save money these days.
But for a while there, most of the major television shows employed a goodly number of major name Jazz musicians.

Well, for instance, all of the shows... I did Danny Kaye's show, and that had... Herb Ellis was in the rhythm section, me and Herb, and Buddy Collette happened to be on that same show. And the Jonathan Winters Show, we did that same one, and they were mostly Jazz musicians, Jazz-orientated musicians. And the Carol Burnett Show, same way. I did four years with Danny Kaye, four years with Carol Burnett (and in between that I'm doing Jonathan Winters), and four years on Flip Wilson's show. So that's twelve years of shows -- live shows, that is, with live audience.
The residuals.
Yes.
Who else besides... Buddy Collette, you say, was...
He played lead alto, and William Green played third alto, and they all doubled tenors and flutes and clarinets and...
Piccolos.
...piccolos and bass clarinets and bassoons, and the whole complement of reeds. I played the tuba and bass on the show, and the Fender bass.
Who else from the Jazz community was on the...
Well, I mentioned Candoli and Buddy Childers.
We were talking about Flip Wilson, but how about some of the other shows that you played? Was it always the same people?
Oh, different people. It's difficult to remember all their names now, because it goes back so many years. I'd have to pull the file out of the back of my brain and get those together.
If they should surface while we're talking, we can get them in.
Okay.
That is a somewhat undocumented part of Jazz musicians' lives on the West Coast.

Yeah. Well, very few people know that most of the musicians who work in the studios are Jazz orientated. Even you find with the string players now... The string players are getting younger and younger, and better and better, although those that have been doing the work for years are all marvelous musicians. You know, I took... Every now and then, someone would want to go on a date, and they'd see how it happened, and they'd just pass the music out and we'd play it, check if there's any wrong notes, then we'd play it, then they'd get a balance and record it right away. Most people think this is amazing, but this is the norm for here.
Red Callender (Patricia Willard) - (8-25-82):

...a couple of other Callenders I ran across. One is Howard Callender, who played trumpet with Eddie Diaz(?) and his Boston Brownies in 1931. You mentioned your family having lived in Boston. I wondered if Howard Callender was any relation of yours.
Well, all the Callenders come from Barbados originally, so...
Or Scotland.
Yes. So he is probably a distant relative. That's from before me. 1931. Howard.
But I wondered if you were aware of him, or...
No, I wasn't aware of him, but I am aware of Charles Callender. He's a trumpet player. I met him.
And I understand he worked with and recorded with Nat Cole in 1939. Someone told me that, I believe. I don't think I could find that in a discography.
It must have been in New York. I don't think he's ever been out here.
But you say you met him?
Yes, I met him when I was in New York, when I was a kid. Well, not exactly a kid, but in the Forties when I was working in the Cafe Society with Lee and Lester's band.
And did you try to establish whether or not you were related?
No, we didn't really set any firm tie. But since all Callenders come from the one island mostly, we figured that we had to be related somehow.
You mentioned at the beginning of the oral history an annual reunion of Callenders.

Yes. That's in Lunenberg, Massachusetts. My cousin, Marcus Callender, who was also a warrant officer in the Army... He conducted a band. He started in Washington, and he conducted an Army band in Germany and all over. He was a very good musician. He has since retired from the Army, and he is going... He just sent me a letter the other day. He's got some sort of a degree in Security, whatever that means. It probably means that he's in charge of security for a bank or something in that town. But he had to go to school to get a degree to do that.
He's the one that organizes the Callender reunion?

Yes, he's the one who organizes that one. There's also another one somewhere in Pennsylvania that I haven't heard about. They call these clan meetings. They happen every year. I guess that's because the Callenders originated in Scotland, like I said. So there seems to be

quite a few of them around now. When I first came here (I might have mentioned this before), I was the only Callender in the whole book. No, there was another one, Jane Callender, who was a tennis player, but she was of another hue.
Do you have a Callender Clan Plaid?
No. We have some sort of a coat of arms. I haven't seen it. I still have yet to show you the genealogy.
You were going to bring that over.
Yeah. I will sometime. It stretches probably 14 feet across the floor. You know, all the "begats" and all that stuff is on it.
That would really be interesting to see.
I'll show it to you.
You said last year when we first started this that you didn't know whether you would be going to the next reunion. Have you been to one since we...

No, I haven't been to one. When they happen... Last year when they had it, I was in Europe, and this year it just wasn't practical to go, because I have to stick around close, because my mother being over 85 and then being an only child, I have to stick close.
Is she living here in Los Angeles?
Oh, yeah.
I don't think I realized that.
Yeah, I talk to her every day.
Wonderful.
Well, she thinks so. She thinks I never did a wrong thing in my life.
I'm sure you didn't!
Well, it would be hard to tell her the truth. She wouldn't believe it anyhow.

Well, we're becoming more and more Callender conscious here lately. I've noticed your name more and more often. A week ago Bill Green's Kansas City 7 broadcast live from the County Museum, and they played Red Callender originals.

I heard it. And I taped it. I wrote them a thank-you note. That's one of the tunes I was telling you about some time ago. It originally started as 'Dolphin Street Boogie,' and then I made a record on it... I said I was copying Duke Ellington. I did a record on it, and called it 'Dedicated To the Blues.' And now with the new title, we call it 'See You Later, So Long.' It now has a lyric.
Oh, that's the one that Mary Lou...
Mary Lou wrote a great lyric to it.
I didn't realize that was the same... When I heard the instrumental version on the radio, I didn't realize it was the same one.
"I'll See You Later, So Long." That's the same one.
Of course. Well, Bill's group did a magnificent job.
Yes, I thought it was very well done.
Absolutely.
I also thought the group was nice.
Yes, it was. It was very good. Bill Green is someone who is certainly deserving of wider recognition.
Yes, he is. He can do it all. Did you ever see him play his bassoon riding a unicycle.
A unicycle? Yes.
Oh, you've seen it. [LAUGHS]
Well, my daughter studied flute with him. Bill used to give us demonstrations. Karate demonstrations, unicycle demonstrations, and we heard him on all the instruments.
He plays all of the reeds equally well. Alto saxophone, tenor, baritone, oboe, bassoon, English horn. He's a marvel.
He really is. And unfortunately, he's not well known away from the studio scene on the West Coast.
Well, that's the problem with the studios. Unless you have nerve enough to get out of the studios and let people know what you do, they'll never know who you are.
His name is not known at all, I don't think, away from here.
No. Well, he hasn't made any records.
He's on a lot.
He's on a lot of records, but not under his own name. And now... You've probably heard the same program I did. He did Coleman Hawkins' version of "Body and Soul."
Yes.

And he does a lot of Charlie Parker originals with the reeds... Well, he does them with different combinations. George Bohannon playing trombone... I think maybe he should do a record on his own, with some new material. I'm not against what he's doing, but I think some new material that would be fresh to people. Because he is a truly marvelous musician.
Yes, he certainly is. And he's been a part of many important bands, as well as recording sessions and soundtracks. He's currently, I believe, playing with Nat Pierce-Randy Capp's Juggernaut.
Oh, is he doing that? He probably is.
I think he just played the Concord Festival with them, and a festival in Oregon. I've seen him in many of the local bands. But he never travels. He never leaves home. Right?

He leaves home, but only... His home is in Kansas City. When he goes, he just goes on a vacation. But he never takes a band out on the road. He's so busy with his students, you know... He's a professional teacher besides being one of the ace studio musicians.
Well, he and Buddy Collette have a woodwind workshop, do they not?
I think that's no longer in effect. Buddy is busy doing a lot of... At the moment, he's working on Hello, Dolly.
The one with Carol Channing?
Carol Channing, yeah.
We have two Hello, Dolly's in the Los Angeles area right now.
There are?
Yeah. Joanne Morley is doing it in Long Beach and Carol Channing is doing it downtown simultaneously.
I worked on the one downtown. I subbed for

Jim Self on tuba the other day. And speaking of studios, I guess everyone has heard of Mort Stephens. He's the guy who did the theme song for Hawaii Five-O and Police Woman and several other shows. Anyhow, business has been rather slow around town, I hear. And I got a call from Dateline(?) just last night. He's got a new TV film coming up, and him being one of the loyal people, naturally he calls me.
[PAUSE]
Oh, I think it's marvelous that people still think of you like that. Whenever he calls me, I play two band dates for him.

Great. I've been listening to the tapes we've done here. We've made multiple references to Buddy Collette, but all of them are just in passing. "Buddy Collette said..." Buddy Collette referred Charles Mingus to you. We haven't really talked about Buddy. I think it might be a good idea to put Buddy into the record, and what Buddy stands for in...
Well, Buddy stands for music of the highest order. Buddy is...
[PAUSE]
...superlatives to describe Buddy Collette, really. Buddy is a marvelous clarinet player, a marvelous flute player, and one of the first people I ever heard play Jazz on flute.
And Buddy also plays all of the reeds... Well, that's the single reeds. He doesn't play oboe and English horn and those, but the flute and the clarinet and all of the saxophones. Buddy has no fears.
But he's somebody else who does not have a big name, because...
Well, Buddy is very well-known.
Well, yes and no. Not to the public. He's well-known to musicians. But I don't think the public... Do you think the public...
Well, not as well as he should be. But he certainly is well known among musicians. He's always busy. He's busier than he needs to be.
Oh, yes. But it's mostly in the studios, and not... He rarely does anything where his name is heard. His music is heard all the time, but unfortunately, not a great many people know that.

Well, at this point, Buddy is busy doing a lot of small gigs. Like, the other night we played a gig for one of the political parties down at a hotel on Wilshire. I guess there's no point mentioning which one, because...
Well, that's all right. You can mention it.
It was the Democratic Party, but personally I don't think there's much difference between the parties.
And this was at what hotel? The Beverly Wilshire?

The Beverly Wilshire. The funny thing, President Reagan was staying in the same hotel, but the Democrats had rented the main ballroom that night, and the Republicans were a little late for that one. So we played there. You know, they're really pushing our Mayor for Governor.
Mayor Bradley, yes.

Mayor Bradley. But we're not talking politics here; only in passing. And the only reason that came up was because Buddy does so many of those kind of gigs, you know. He has I guess you'd say the type of personality that fits in. Buddy is a very gregarious type, and whether he is known to the public or not, he certainly is known to everybody in this area.
Well, he received a couple of awards from the American Civil Liberties Union, I know -- he's been honored by them.
Yes.
And they've given fundraisers and they've presented him in concerts. But he hasn't been presented
often enough as a leader or as an individual musician or composer.

And he's great at all those things. He's written music for some pictures, which you see every now and then on the Late, Late Show. He's a very prolific writer and a player. I can't think of enough nice things to say about Buddy Collette.
He's been a mover in the music community here from the time he was a youngster. He was one of the people who worked very hard to amalgamate...
In the amalgamation of the unions. Yes, he was there.
And he was one of the first Black musicians in the studios.
He was probably the first.
Well, that's what I had heard for a long time. Then Marshall Royal told me that he'd worked in the movie studios. But Buddy worked in the television and radio studios.
Yeah, well, I worked in the movie studios way back in the early Forties. I was reading in one of your books here, I Dood It, that was in 1943, with Hazel Scott and Lee Young...
Lena Horne, Hazel Scott, Lee Young, Jimmy Dorsey, John O'Connell, Bob Eberle and Barney Bigard. Those were the list of names in the book. But you and Barney, among other musicians...
Well, Lee and I were featured with Hazel Scott in that particular picture...
[PAUSE]
...seeing the picture.
It was a Red Skelton picture.
1943. At MGM.
Do you remember what other Jazz musicians were involved besides you and Lee Young?
Not really. You know, all I was concerned with, all we were concerned with was our little segment.
On Hazel Scott.
And that was Hazel Scott, Lee Young and myself. We had a very nice featured spot in that picture. I know it's way before your time, but...
I was going to movies in 1943, but I may not have been aware of whom I was seeing. Your picture credits: The first one, listed in the index, but not listed in the listing, was St. Louis Blues.
With Nat Cole.
We're talking about the book Jazz and The Movies by David Meeker.
That was one with Nat Cole, where Nat played the part of W.C. Handy. I think Eartha Kitt was also in that picture -- although she's not a Jazz singer, but she was in the picture.
Was that your first film?

Oh, no. My first film that I remember being in was when I first got here, in I think 1937, a thing called Think Fast, Mr. Moto, with Peter Lorre. I was just a sideline musician, but I was in it anyhow. That one wasn't listed, because they didn't call that "Jazz" in those days. See, "Jazz" has been a dirty name for pictures.
Yes.
As a matter of fact, I didn't start to make any money until I disassociated my name from Jazz -- so to speak.
You mean when you played with the Symphony in Hawaii?

Well, really, yeah. People always thought Jazz musicians couldn't read, you know. When I first started working in pictures, the contractors... A conductor would ask for me, and the contractor would call because it was his duty to call, and he'd say, "By the way, do you have
a bow and do you read music?" Which could have been insulting, but I took it, you know, that they didn't know any better.
Did you do any films between 1937 and I Dood It?
Between 1937 and 1943?
Yes.

Yeah, I did a lot of sideline in pictures. As a matter of fact, I just remembered one, some Jungle picture. Nat Cole and I were both in the picture, Lee Young also. The funny thing about pictures in those days, they'd call typical Black musicians or typical Black people, and sometimes I didn't fit the typical role because I had red hair and freckles, so they'd stick me way in the background!
We could hear you but we couldn't see you?
Yeah. Well, it was sideline stuff. But it was fun. You know, all of it was fun, and we'd have a ball just being there.
You don't remember the names of any of those pictures in that period.
No, at the present I can't think of any of the names. There was just a whole raft of them.
Then the other ones listed in Meeker's book were the Life of Riley in 1949...
Life of Riley, yeah. That was my first steady show. That was the one with Jerry Fielding.
Oh, you mentioned that before.

I mentioned that before, yes. That was about the same time Buddy Collette... Well, it was a little after Buddy was hired to do the Groucho Marx Show. That's when Jerry Fielding really bit off a big chunk when he decided to use two Black musicians on his shows, you know. They thought that... Well, he was called a Communist for doing that. Which was ridiculous, but that was the word, you know. "What right has he to hire Black people, where he's taking work away from good White people?" It wasn't like that at all. He just hired us because he liked the way we played.

I think that was one of the things that led to Buddy's determination to do something about amalgamation. When he found out that the contractor on the show wouldn't give him a W-2 and wouldn't give him...
Yes, he had to go over on Central Avenue to pick up his check or something like that.
He was not treated the same as the other musicians because the contractor was a member of Local 47, and Buddy was 767.
Yes...
[PAUSE]

I was also a member of 767, just like Buddy. But fortunately, it didn't stop people from calling us to work in pictures, just because there were two locals. They wanted whatever particular talent we had, and a lot of them had nerve enough to call us. Nelson Riddle was another one who didn't let the fact that there was two unions deter him from calling whoever he wanted.

And Greg McRitchie(?) was another one. I used to do that show, You Asked For It. There's a new one on now, but the old one, I was on that one, too. That was an interesting show inasmuch as everything was filed beforehand, and then they'd add the dialogue... That was at ABC, incidentally. They'd add the dialogue after, and we'd sit in a little room and play music on cue. For instance, if they were showing a circus scene, the music might be... [SINGS FAMOUS CIRCUS THEME]. And Greg McRitchie was the conductor on that show. He was another guy who didn't let the fact that our hues were different deter him from calling us.
He was a nice man. He came out of the Big Band Era. He came out of what band... I interviewed him once for a liner note...
Yes, he's one of the beautiful people.
Yes, nice man. Nice man. After those films you did Jammin' The Blues?
Jammin' The Blues was in 1944 or '5, somewhere in there.
Lester Young...
Lester Young, Sweets Edison, Jo Jones, Illinois Jacquet...
Barney Kessel...
Barney Kessel.
Marlowe Morris.
Marlowe Morris played piano in that.
John Simmons.
John Simmons.
Big Sid and Marie Bryant.

Yeah, Marie Bryant who was like Louis Armstrong's number-one fan. She did "Sunny Side of the Street" in that. The funny thing, my first record (I mentioned this before) was with Louis Armstrong, and it was
"Sunny Side of the Street" -- and Marie Bryant did it exactly like Louis did it.
She was (?).
Yes, she was. She was a great dancer, too.
Oh, I know, yes. She danced in Jump For Joy.
That's right.
In later years she was the choreographer on Pearl Bailey's show, Pearl Bailey's talent show on ABC.
She left us a few years ago, didn't she.
Yes, just a very few, about three years ago, I think.
That recent, huh?
Yes.
Yes, we used to hang out together. She and the...what's the trumpet player who was with Duke...
Ray Nance.
Ray Nance.
They had a daughter.
Yes, they did have a daughter. I imagine she's still...
She's a nurse, in Pasadena, I think. She has three children...
That's funny. I never met the daughter, as well as I knew Marie and Ray.

I don't think I have either. I've talked to her on the telephone, but I've never met her. I don't know her married name either. In fact, I've looked for her. Marl Young told me he'd find her for me, because Marl knows her, but Marl can't remember her married name either.
[END OF CASSETTE 5, SIDE A]
Marl is running for President of the Union. I don't know if you know that.
Yes. He made the front page of Variety. I mean, I saw it in Overture, but Variety scooped Overture. Overture being Local 47's monthly newspaper.
I think he'll make it. Certainly he's very... He's over-qualified.
Absolutely. With his connections, he could do... He can achieve great things, I think, because he is...
I'm sure.
He operates on multiple levels, and he's a member of...
Everything.
...the State Arts Council... From Federal, State, City and County, he's involved in every level of the Arts.
Yeah. He's the type of guy that seems to be able to handle everything. I marvel at people like Marl and also our beloved Mayor. I don't see how these people ever rest!
I don't either. Currently, Marl's actual title is Secretary of Local 47. Of course, he's the former musical director for the Lucille Ball Show...
Yes, the Lucille Ball Show, right. And that's another first. He was the first Black conductor on any major show.
And way back in Chicago, Charlie Parker used to work for him, he told me.
True.
So Marl brings unique qualifications.
Besides being politically motivated, he's also a tremendous arranger, and just a great musician.
Right. A pianist...
Mmm-hmm. So I guess his playing days are over. If he gets to be President, he won't have time to play any more.
I guess. Well, does he have time now?
No.
I haven't heard him play for a long, long time.
He's been threatening, but I don't think he'll get around to it.
But he certainly achieves a lot, which is marvelous.
He really does.
You also... We talked about Blazing Saddles.
Did we?
Yes, on another reel. Your brief moment in the desert with Count Basie.
In the desert, in the wind, high winds, and dust with Count Basie. It was fun just being there. Being anywhere in Count Basie's presence is an honor to me.
Right. And most recently he saw you twice last week at Disneyland.
Well, whenever he's within a hundred miles, I make it.
Well, we all do.
That was a 200-mile round-trip to Disneyland, but...
From where you live out in the San Fernando Valley out to Anaheim in Orange County, it was a trip.
I don't care. Anywhere he is, I'll be.
Well, he has a good band.
A great band!
We also had a listing in this book for New Orleans, 1947.
That was the picture with Louis. Did we talk about that before?

I believe we talked about this picture in Jazz People where you identified all the musicians. But interestingly, in this book Jazz In The Movies, there is another picture, apparently taken at the same time with the same musicians, but it's a different shot... But the thing that makes it even more interesting than the one in Jazz People is the other people that show in the picture on the set. And you identified some of them that you remember. Mantan Moreland.
That's Mantan; he was a chef. And that's Clarence Landry; they called him Frenchy...
He was in Jump For Joy.
Jump For Joy. And that's Susan Harbin...
Who was also in Jump For Joy.
Mmm-hmm, and who's married to the great artist Calvin Bailey, who is my... Calvin and I went to school together...
Which school?
In the Indiana Avenue school in Atlantic City, New Jersey. I didn't mention him. He was a few years ahead of me, but as you grow up and older you forget the little distance in age there.
Well, I didn't know you and Calvin went back that far. I knew you were tight friends.
Yeah. Well, we were kids together.
I know Cal always does your Christmas cards, the sketches of you on it, that there's really no mistake about whose Christmas card that is. And Cal did a record album cover for you, too, didn't he?
Yeah, he did. When we had...Buddy and Al Viola and Al Aarons and Grover Mitchell and Leroy Vinnegar had a label together. He did our album covers for us.
That's Calvin Cornelius Bailey, right?
You knew his middle name, Cornelius!
Yes, he's a fine artist, and caricaturist. I mean, he does marvelous caricatures.
You know, he retired, but he's gone back to work.
He retired?! I didn't know that.
Oh, you didn't know that? Yeah, he couldn't stay retired. He just couldn't stand the inactivity. So he's back at his old stand at...
Universal?
At Universal.

Well, I first met Calvin at the Hollywood Empire, the club that Gene Norman ran in Hollywood, and Calvin not only was doing...he wandered around in his cap and gown like a graduate, doing caricatures of the customers, but that was just sort of a sideline. His real pleasure was the music, and drawing some caricatures of the artists in there. He did caricatures of everybody in Duke's band in 1949, and Duke was so enthralled with his work that he asked for all the caricatures -- and I believe Calvin gave them to him. Duke told me he was going to put them in his book, but they weren't in Music Is My Mistress. So we don't know what's happened to them. Cal and I wondered.
That's a great waste, because Calvin Bailey is truly... In what he does he has no fears; he's great at it.
That's right.
I was looking at this picture here from New Orleans, and I see Zuttie Singleton, Kid Ory, Bud Scott,
Louis Armstrong, Barney Bigard, Charlie Beal and myself -- and there's only two of us left out of that bunch.
You and Charlie. Yes. And that was 1947.
You were mentioning also another film that you were in that's not listed in the book, and that's Gypsy. Isn't that right?

Oh, I played in the background music in that picture, with Rosalind Russell. The thing that stands out in my mind about that is that Rosalind Russell actually sang some of the songs. You know, she wasn't really a singer, and so we probably did about 46 takes on one thing that she did, and they pieced it together, and you know, they do marvelous...they do magic with the scissors out in the studios -- so she came over just great. I saw it... The picture was on the other night, in the Natalie Wood series that was going on. Natalie was actually Gypsy, and Rosalind Russell was her mother, who was a typical stage mother -- at least that was the role she played.
Were there other Jazz musicians on that film?
Let's see. I think it was Shelly Manne and I, and I can't remember who else was on it. I remember
Shelley because... Well, everybody remembers Shelly that works with him.
Right. Nice man.
Beautiful man.
What year was this? Do you remember?
That was around 1965, I think. And another funny thing happened. I know you've heard of Carmen Cavallero.
Of course.

Well, on Decca, Shelley and I did a trio date with him, just piano, bass and drums. And Carmen Cavallero was I guess you'd say a perfectionist. We did actually 46 whole takes on a tune because there was some little run that he wasn't quite satisfied with. I don't think you'll find that in the discographies anywhere, but that was another thing that Shelley and I...I shouldn't say "suffered through," but it did get difficult -- to do 46 complete takes on one tune.
I guess! Then your other film that is listed is St. Louis Blues in 1958.
That was the story of W.C. Handy, right?
Right.
And Nat Cole had the title role.

Right. And it also features Pearl Bailey, Cab Calloway, Mahalia Jackson, Ella Fitzgerald, Barney Bigard, Teddy Buckner, Red Callender, Curtis Counce, Lee Young, and Billy Preston as the boy W.C. Handy, music arranged and conducted by Nelson Riddle.
Yeah, I mentioned Nelson before.
Right. So you worked with Barney on several pictures, right?

Oh, yeah. Over the years I suppose I worked with Barney quite a bit. Many records dating back to The Lamp-Lighter, when Kay Starr first started. We did all of her original things. You've heard of the Lamp-Lighter.
Oh, yes.
What was his name? Ted Yertzer(?).
Yes, right.
He was also a writer for one of the daily papers here.
Wasn't it the Times? I can't remember.
I think it was the Daily News.
Yes, that's right.

And he was a real Jazz buff, or fan as they say now. But he loved us all. I remember Allan Reuss, Zutty Singleton and Barney Bigard and Barney Kessel. But we used to record almost every day. We'd all get through work
at night, and there was some place on Kowanga(?) Boulevard...I don't remember the name of it. But that's where we'd meet every night and record with Kay Starr and whoever else.
Record every night?
Every night. This man just loved music.
Every night for how long?

Oh, for weeks. Oh yeah, we made probably 50 or 75 sides at least with this one label. I don't know who has all the masters. He released quite a few of them, but I know there's a lot of them that never saw the light of day. So they're still around somewhere. That's when 78's were the big deal. They'll turn up somewhere.
You mentioned something a minute ago when I was changing the tapes about going to Las Vegas with Lena Horne. Tell me about that.
That was in 1947. The Flamingo... Did I mention the Last Frontier? But it was the Flamingo.
Well, you mentioned Bugsy Siegel, and Bugsy Siegel was connected with...

Well, Bugsy Siegel was the owner. At least he was supposed to have been the owner. And Xavier Cugat's band was featured, and was it Lynn René... I've forgotten who... Was that the name of the girl in that film we looked
at a minute ago? Anyhow, Xavier Cugat's was the featured orchestra...
Oh, Lena Romai(?).

Lena Romai(?). Xavier Cugat's band was the featured orchestra, and Lena Horne was the featured attraction. And she took Arnold Ross and Irving Ashby and myself. We were her trio. And we actually saw the incident which has been in a few books, where a waiter dropped a plate or made some noise, and Bugsy Siegel literally kicked the guy out of the room. And that was during... During that period in Las Vegas, Blacks couldn't stay on whatever side of town it was. We stayed over in a place called the Dust Bowl.
On the West Side.
Was that the West Side. Well, wherever it was, that's where the Black musicians had to...
It was called the Dust Bowl the streets were not paved...

The streets were not paved, right. And we stayed at...I think the lady's house was Miss Harris. So Arnold Ross, who I love dearly, refused to stay... He could have stayed anywhere, but he decided he was going to stay with us, because we were together. So we all shared one room with I guess three beds in the room, but that's the

best we could do at that time. And Lena had... Well, they gave Lena a cabin or whatever you call it, a motor-home or something in back of the Flamingo. That's when things were really mean. You had to go in the back door... That is, the Black musicians had to go in the back door, and well, we were...
And stay in the back.
And stay in the back, yeah. When you got through, you couldn't go in the dining room. That's what being invisible means, I suppose.
Wasn't it around that same period that Hazel Scott (I think it was Hazel Scott) decided to take a swim in the pool, and dove into the pool, and they drained the pool?
I heard about that, but I didn't see that.
Well, I just heard about it, too. But that was around that time, wasn't it?

It figures. It had to be around that time. Anyhow, Lena and I one day went downtown to see a show. I think Orson Welles' new picture had just come out, Citizen Kane [sic]. And we went in they show, and they took our money, but when we got in the show they put us way over on the side, so the picture looked like it was coming at you from an angle. So we went back out and got our money back.
And after that engagement I said I'd never go to Las Vegas again, and so I didn't. That was in '47. I didn't go to Las Vegas any more until 1969.
Good for you.
And I still don't like Las Vegas.
I don't either. But by 1969...
Well, everything was cool by then.
Because they fixed things pretty much in the early 1960's...
Well, they didn't want Martin Luther King marching in Las Vegas, so overnight it changed.
Well, the NAACP said that they had 600 people prepared to come and sit in in every lobby in every major hotel on the Strip, and that panicked the hotel owners, and they came around.
Yeah. So nothing drastic happened. They just... You know, people are people. Just as usual. They might have made a little more money...!
Right!

But that soured me on Las Vegas. I've never felt the same about it. And that's one reason I've spent most of my career never going South, until 1974. Twentieth Century Fox called me out for an interview one day, and they wanted me to play the bandleader in a picture about Buddy

Holly, and they were shooting this picture in Jackson, Mississippi. And I said, "Are you sure it's cool in Jackson, Mississippi?" So they assured me that everything would be fine, and sure enough, it was. I went to Jackson, Mississippi, and I was just treated beautifully. But we stayed in the Jacksonian Hotel, the whole film company did. But after talking to some of the locals, I discovered that if it hadn't been Twentieth Century Fox, it would have been a different story.
Oh yeah?
Oh yeah.
This was what...
Was this The Buddy Holly Story.

It was The Buddy Holly Story. But that one was cancelled, because Buddy Holly's widow didn't... They hadn't gotten things straight with her, and she had an attorney, and after they had spent a couple of million dollars they scrubbed the whole project. And later Paramount did the story.
Did they go ahead and make the picture, and then...
No, we did about three weeks, then they called the whole thing off. So whatever we did is still in
the can at Fox. And she made a deal with Paramount, and I understand it's been a very successful picture.
That's what I heard, too.

The funny thing about it is...what was it...I forget the name of the group... But anyhow, this was a group out of Lubbock, Texas, originally, and they sang Rock-and-Roll, and the bookers thought it was a Black group, and they booked them into the Apollo Theater. So I play the part of the bandleader from the Apollo Theater. That's how the whole story took place. It was a very... You know, it was fun doing it. It was a very interesting story, and I was sorry it got cancelled. But it didn't hurt too much, because I became a member of the Screen Actors Guild through that, so every time I work in any picture capacity I get Screen Actors Guild money, which is a lot different than musicians' money!
Well, I'm glad there was a happy ending!
Oh, yeah. Everything turned out all right, and I wasn't strung up.

Tell me about your instruments. You mentioned that on your job with Louis Armstrong, you had just gotten one of the basses that you still have. Where did you get it? You also mentioned another time that Mingus willed his bass to you.
Yeah, Mingus willed his bass to me. That was a few years ago, whenever he died...
Almost three years ago, I think.

At least. I got a letter from his estate attorney, and it was a big surprise: "Charles Mingus has willed his Roth bass to one Red Callender." So I went to New York and checked it out, and I brought it back. It was just that simple.
You have that one. You have the one that you played with Louis Armstrong.

I have that one and the one that I played with Louis Armstrong. I got that bass on the 12th of November in 1937, and the next night was the night I opened with Louis Armstrong -- and I still have that same instrument.
Where did you get that instrument?
There was a store on Lower Broadway in Los Angeles at that time called Locky(?) Music. You might have heard of that. I don't think it's in existence any longer.
All the musicians went there.

Yes. But there was a salesman there named Uly Apfell, who for some reason took a liking to me, and he says, "Hey, kid, I've got this Morelli bass from Germany, and I think you should have it." So I went down and got it.
It took me about three years to pay for it. And I still have that one.

I'm going to jump ahead, because this concerns the same person, Uly Apfell. He had his own music store on 9th and Broadway in 1948 or '49. Anyhow, when I came back from Honolulu in 1950, I went to see him, and he had another Morelli, which is a very good instrument, and he said, "I think you should have this one, too" -- and I bought that one.
So I have the two Morellis, and the Roth that Mingus left me, and another little Roblès, a Mexican bass that I have. So I have four basses and five tubas, and I've got a room I can hardly get in!
Tell me about the five tubas. How do they differ?

Well, Uly Apfell is in this story, too. Because people didn't know I played tuba for many years when I came here. He had a big Conn tuba, and so I went and bought it, and I used to go out in Hollywood Hills, just by myself, every day, until I got myself really together, and then I made an album called Callender Speaks Low, and that's how I let people know I played tuba. Ever since that time I started getting studio calls with the tuba and the bass. So the tuba has been just as important in my life as the bass.
That was the first one I bought. Then Yamaha gave me two tubas, and King gave me a tuba. That accounts for four.

And a friend of mine, the widow of Bob Short, who used to play with Bob Scobie's band, had... He's since deceased, too. He got killed in a flying accident. Anyhow, she's a friend of my wife's, Mary Lou's. In the closet she had a couple of paper bags, and in these paper bags was a tuba. So I brought them back and took them over to George Strusell at Mirophone, and he put this horn together. It's a beautiful instrument. It was made in 1859. The funny thing about it, it's made by Augustus Bopp.
What a great name!

Yeah. In Munich, Germany. Augustus Bopp, Munich, Germany, 1859. I think this was an old German calvary horn. Anyway, it's a beautiful-sounding instrument, ancient, but... George Strusell, who has since moved to Sweden, put this instrument together and made it work. He's an amazing technician with brass instruments. Since he's gone, there's another one here, Larry Kimick, who is in Culver City on Sepulveda Boulevard, who is an excellent repair guy.
So that accounts for my five tubas.
Uly Apfell is spelled?
Uly Apfell. He's since deceased, too. But he was another one of the beautiful people.
Another thing I don't think I got around to asking you was when you and Mary Lou got married.
Eleven years ago, the 29th of this month, August. We lived together for about three years before that, and then we decided, "Well, I think it's going to be okay."
Looks like it!
Yeah.
What was Mary Lou's name before?
Lyons. Well, she was an original member of the Cheerleaders. Did you ever hear of them?
Yes.

Herman McCoy used to lead a singing group. That's where I first met her, at...was it UCLA? We rehearsed at UCLA. We rehearsed with June Christy, Buddy Collette again, Nelson Riddle and myself -- somehow we were featured with this group. Nelson had the band, because he had already quit playing trombone, he was just writing. But we were the featured artists along with Herman McCoy and this group, and Mary Lou was a member of the group. That's where I first met her.
And Herman McCoy is a choir director and vocal arranger who once worked with Lionel Hampton...
The same.
He says that his real name is not really Herman, but Harmony.
Harmony.
That's what he says. Harmony McCoy.
I believe him.
Well, why not? He's a great talent.
Oh, he's a marvelous talent!
And he cooks good, too.
Yeah, I think that's what he's doing now.
Is it at the Golden Door?
I'm not sure where, but if you ever find out, let me know. I'd like to go see him.
I know he did a diet cookbook, if you can believe that.
A diet cookbook?
And I know he cooks rich, because everything I've ever tasted that he cooks is...
Oh, lots of butter...
Extremely delicious! Not dietetic at all.
Well, I have to credit Herman McCoy with bringing Mary Lou and I together.
I didn't realize that.
Well, I hadn't thought about it like that, but he was the real reason.
And she told me she worked in Las Vegas.
She worked with Betty Hutton. She worked the Betty Hutton show at the Tropicana.
She was a backup singer?

She was a backup singer, a dancer (she danced, too), and she also was featured with Ray Conniff's orchestra as a featured vocalist. And now she's up at Daylight (?) studying guitar. You didn't know that.
No, I didn't know that.

She's studying with Dave Koonce. He's a marvelous musician. We worked together recently, he and Gerry Wiggins and I. Gerry Wiggins and I and Harold Jones worked with Buddy Collette last night. When I left home, I was really exhausted, but Gerry brings me to life, just listening to him play.
Ah, he's magnificent.
Isn't he magnificent?
And I am with Mary Lou. We think we've got to find a room for you and Gerry to just play. A beautiful, relaxing, comfortable...
That's what it will be. Relaxed!
I think that would be so great!
Yeah, we get along. There seems to be a mutual admiration, you know. I love his playing, and he tells me he likes mine -- so that makes me float around, you know.
Well, you both have good taste.
Well, thank you.
Tell me about your grants. You've gotten several now, right?
Yes. The latest one was for composing.
These were National Endowment For the Arts Jazz Grants.
NEA, yeah. Mmm-hmm. And I must thank you or somebody...
I was not involved in the last one.
You didn't have anything to do with that.
Earlier ones, yes, but the last one, no.
Well, somebody was looking out for me, because it came not too long ago. And it's marvelous that somebody cares over there.
Well, they recognize quality. They're good people.
Well, I'm so happy about it, because...
This is a composing grant, and you're...
I'm already into it. I'm writing every day.
What are you writing?
Oh, a bunch of original things. Well, naturally it would be original if I write them.
Is it a single large work, or...

Well, my original title for the whole work is Jazz Travels, which, you know, can cover everything, because Jazz does travel. It has to travel to exist! So one thing I've completed is a thing called "Merry-Go-Round." I just took it to a professional copyist. I'll give you a copy. Today he brought it to me. That's one that's finished.
Didn't Mary Lou do a lyric?
Yes, Mary Lou did the lyric. Did you hear it?
Yes, I heard it.
Well, that's the one. I just finished revising it, and now it's complete.
Oh, I loved that.
Oh, I'm glad. Because that will be a part of it. Whenever it's performed, that will be in it.
And you had a performance grant. This was your second or third?
Well, the Smithsonian and the other one... performance...
And that resulted in a concert that we've talked about that was at Santa Monica in the Spring.
Yes. And this composer's grant, I don't have to do a concert, but I intend to.
Oh, please. Please do.
Yeah. I either want to do it at Santa Barbara or maybe San Diego State College.

Oh, incidentally, I was at a Black History in the University of California, Santa Barbara, about a month ago. Professor Douglas Daniels, who is a young Black History professor up there, invited me to talk to the class. It's summer school, and I guess there were between 18 and 20 people in the class, and I think out of 18 to 20 there were 6 or 7 Black students. And I asked if anybody had ever heard of Charlie Parker, and nobody had ever heard of Charlie Parker except for one kid who was in high school -- he happened to be sitting in the class. And none of them had heard of Art Tatum. I thought this was pathetic. So I
asked everybody who had not heard of Art Tatum to come and write his name on a notebook I had. So I sent them all Art Tatum albums, thanks to Norman Granz.
Oh, how wonderful.

Yeah. And I got a couple of letters from them, and they said it was marvelous. But strange thing, one letter said that he thought Art Tatum was great but he'd rather hear Benny Carter. I sent him the Benny Carter. Which was nice, you know, but the fact that these people could have lived in this century and not heard of Art Tatum was rather devastating.
Somebody ought to be teaching, or exposing them. Thank you for doing it.

Well, that's one of my jobs. So I have to go back up there when the Fall season starts, and I have to go down to San Diego to do another one. That's my job, to tell people about Black history -- music history, that is. Because having been a part of it, and still a part of it, I do know a little about what happened, and these kids should know. Because without these people, who would know? Down at the college in Santa Monica, the head of the English class told me she'd put up a question and asked who Louis Armstrong was. And you'd be surprised at some of the
answers she got. One of the most fascinating was "the first man on the Moon."
Well, maybe! Then along came Neal.
Yeah. But they don't teach anything in... They're sadly lacking in what's being taught these days. They seem to just want to push the kids through, and half of them can't even read.
And they get no chance at exposure anywhere else, certainly not from the radio.

No. There's only... Well, there's one station on FM that plays Jazz, sometimes, and there's two on AM, KGIL, and there's another that's in the Valley, and there's another one in West Covina. They play the old... Which I have nothing against. They play the old Swing. They call it "The Swinging Years," which is better than nothing.
Right. But if the kids don't know where to look for that music, they'll never hear it.
No.
And too many of them have never heard it.
Sadly, too many of them will never get to hear it. So if I can just reach a few of them, just a few... You know, I was thinking, maybe one of the grants
should think about that aspect of history. It's needed, and there's nobody doing it.
Absolutely. If you've got a plan...
I have a plan, and I don't have it with me, but I have a program all worked out.

Then please do it, because it's terribly important. During my term of service on the panel, anyone who came up with a well-designed project for disseminating the music to young people had a good chance. I mean, we wanted to award the grants to those kinds of projects. I don't know how it operates now because I know the budget is cut tremendously. But it's terribly important.

But after this session is over, after this administration is through, maybe something will loosen up a little. I'm counting on it, because everything is cut to the bone now and there's no money to do anything.
We're almost out of tape...
